**Instructions.** Submit a single PDF rendered from a Quarto or RMarkdown source, together with the source file. Each part pairs a published study with an analysis you run yourself on public data. Use the functions from Labs 12 and 13; every question can be answered with code from those labs. You may use AI assistance, but you are responsible for every line you submit. Use `set.seed(723)` before every step that involves randomness (a split, cross-validation, a forest, cross-fitting). Your numbers will differ a little from your classmates' depending on package versions; what is graded is the code, the reading of the output, and the reasoning.

**Data.** Each part opens with a code chunk that loads its data and packages; copy it into your own file. Part 2 needs `ddml` version 0.9 or later, installed from GitHub as in Lab 13:

# Part 1: Prediction

## Read: how predictable is a life?

Salganik et al. (2020, *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*) ask how well life outcomes can be predicted from rich data. The Fragile Families study followed 4,242 families from a child's birth; by age 9 it held 12,942 variables on each family. The authors released the age-15 outcomes for half of the families and invited researchers to predict them for the rest. 160 teams submitted predictions, built with everything from OLS to deep networks. Each submission was scored by its $R^2$ on families whose outcomes no team had seen.

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\small
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.1}
\begin{tabular}{lc@{\hskip 3em}lc}
\toprule
outcome at age 15 & best $R^2$ & outcome at age 15 & best $R^2$ \\
\midrule
material hardship & 0.23 & eviction & 0.05 \\
child's GPA & 0.19 & caregiver's job training & 0.05 \\
child's grit & 0.06 & caregiver's layoff & 0.03 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
```

The best submission was only slightly better than a benchmark chosen by a domain expert: a regression on four variables (the mother's race, marital status, and education at the birth, and the same outcome measured at age 9).

1.  **Reading the design.**

    (a) Why were teams scored on families whose outcomes they never saw, and not on the families they trained on? What would the $R^2$ of a very flexible model look like on its own training families?

    (b) A reader concludes: "With an $R^2$ of 0.2, family background hardly matters for children's lives." Give one reason the conclusion does not follow from a low $R^2$.

## Run: predicting a career in low-wage work

We ask the same question of the NLSY79 extract from Lab 13 (Brand et al. 2021): 4,113 respondents aged 14--17 in 1979 who finished at least 12th grade. The outcome `lowwage` is the share of survey years, 1990--2014, in which the respondent's hourly wage was below two-thirds of that year's median. The predictors are 24 columns measured in adolescence, before anyone could have finished college. They are listed in `xvars`; `ability` is the standardized AFQT score, `parinc` parents' income, `rotter` a locus-of-control scale, `schooldis` a measure of school disadvantage, and the three `_miss` columns flag imputed values. Do not use `college` in this part.

```{r}
library(glmnet); library(rpart); library(ranger)
library(xgboost); library(nnet)
u <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wenhaojiangsoc/",
            "SOCIOL723/main/Data/nlsy79_brand.rds")
d <- readRDS(url(u))
xvars <- c("male", "black", "hispanic", "south", "rural", "parinc",
           "fatheduc", "motheduc", "fatherwc", "twoparent", "siblings",
           "ability", "collegeprep", "rotter", "delinq", "expect",
           "aspire", "friendasp", "schooldis", "married18", "child18",
           "parinc_miss", "schooldis_miss", "fatheduc_miss")
y  <- d$lowwage
Xm <- as.matrix(d[, xvars])                  ## the 24 columns
Xb <- model.matrix(~ .^2, d[, xvars])[, -1]  ## plus every pairwise product
Xb <- Xb[, apply(Xb, 2, var) > 0]            ## drop constant columns
Xb <- Xb[, !duplicated(t(Xb))]               ## drop duplicated columns
## 30% test set: used only to report each model's final R2
set.seed(723)
n  <- nrow(d)
te <- sample(n, round(0.3 * n)); tr <- setdiff(1:n, te)
r2 <- function(pred) {
  1 - mean((y[te] - pred)^2) / mean((y[te] - mean(y[tr]))^2)
}
## data frames for rpart, ranger, and lm
dtr <- data.frame(y = y[tr], Xm[tr, ]); dte <- data.frame(Xm[te, ])
```

2.  **Benchmarks, and what flexibility costs.**

    (a) In the spirit of the four-variable benchmark, fit OLS of `y` on `male`, `black`, `motheduc`, and `ability` on the training cases. Then fit OLS on all 24 columns. Report both test $R^2$.

    (b) Fit OLS on the expanded design `Xb` (use `lm.fit(cbind(1, Xb[tr, ]), y[tr])` as in Lab 12's scoreboard, and set any `NA` coefficient to 0 before predicting). Report its $R^2$ on the *training* cases and on the test cases. Explain the gap, and the comparison with (a), in terms of bias and variance.

3.  **Regularization.**

    (a) Fit the lasso on the 24 columns with `cv.glmnet`. Which variables does it keep at `lambda.1se`? How many at `lambda.min`? Report the test $R^2$ under each rule and say which rule you would use if the goal were prediction, and which if you wanted a short list of predictors to describe.

    (b) Fit the lasso and ridge on `Xb`, with $\lambda$ at `lambda.min`. Report both test $R^2$ and compare them with 2(b). The three models use the same columns. Why do the penalized ones predict better?

4.  **Trees, forests, boosting, and a network.**

    (a) Grow a large tree with `rpart` (`cp = 0.001`) and prune it at the `cp` with the smallest cross-validated error. How many leaves are left? Describe the first two levels of splits in words. Report the test $R^2$.

    (b) Fit a random forest with `ranger` (1,000 trees, `importance = "permutation"`). Then tune it: compute the out-of-bag MSE for `mtry` in (1, 2, 4, 8, 24) and `min.node.size` in (5, 20, 50, 100), and refit at the best pair. Show the grid. Report the test $R^2$ of the default and the tuned forest, and the five variables with the largest permutation importance. Why is the out-of-bag error an honest guide here, when the training error is not?

    (c) Fit boosted trees with `xgboost` (`eta = 0.05`, `max_depth = 3`), choosing the number of steps with `xgb.cv` and early stopping as in Lab 12. How many steps does it choose? Report the test $R^2$.

    (d) Fit a network with one hidden layer of two units with `nnet` (`decay = 1`, `linout = TRUE`, `maxit = 500`) on standardized inputs, using means and standard deviations from the training cases only. Average the predictions of five random starts. Report the test $R^2$.

5.  **The scoreboard.**

    (a) Put every test $R^2$ from questions 2--4 in one sorted table.

    (b) By how much does your best method beat the four-variable benchmark? Compare the pattern with the Fragile Families Challenge in two or three sentences.

    (c) `ability` and `male` lead the importance ranking. A policy memo reads: "Raising adolescents' test scores would move them out of low-wage work." Rewrite the sentence so that it says only what a prediction model can support, and name what would be needed to support the original.

    (d) Suppose you had chosen the forest's `mtry` by its test $R^2$ instead of the out-of-bag error, and then reported that same test $R^2$. What would be wrong with the reported number?

# Part 2: Double Machine Learning

## Read: college and low-wage work

Brand, Xu, Koch, and Geraldo (2021, *Sociological Methodology*) ask whether finishing a four-year college degree by age 25 keeps people out of low-wage work, and for whom. College is not assigned at random, so they compare graduates and non-graduates who share the same pre-college characteristics: the 24 columns of Part 1. Part 1 asked how well those columns *predict* low-wage work. Part 2 uses the same kind of prediction for a different purpose: to estimate the effect of `college` on `lowwage`.

1.  **Reading the design.**

    (a) State, in words, the assumption under which adjusting for the 24 columns identifies the effect of college on low-wage work. Name one variable not on the list that would violate it, and say in which direction it would bias the estimate.

    (b) OLS of `lowwage` on `college` and the 24 columns also "adjusts for" them. What does OLS assume that DML does not? Which assumption do the two share?

## Run: one number, three ways

Use the data from Part 1, all 4,113 respondents, unweighted.

```{r}
library(DoubleML); library(mlr3); library(mlr3learners); library(sandwich)
lgr::get_logger("mlr3")$set_threshold("warn")
dat <- DoubleMLData$new(
  data.table::as.data.table(d[, c("lowwage", "college", xvars)]),
  y_col = "lowwage", d_cols = "college", x_cols = xvars)
learners <- list(
  lasso    = lrn("regr.cv_glmnet", alpha = 1, s = "lambda.min"),
  forest   = lrn("regr.ranger", num.trees = 500),
  boosting = lrn("regr.xgboost", nrounds = 200, eta = 0.05,
                 max_depth = 2))
```

2.  **From OLS to DML.**

    (a) Report the difference in mean `lowwage` between graduates and non-graduates, and the coefficient on `college` from OLS with the 24 columns entered linearly, each with a robust (HC1) standard error.

    (b) For each of the three learners (the same learner for $Y$ and for $D$), fit `DoubleMLPLR` with 5 folds and the folds redrawn 5 times (`n_rep = 5`), keeping the predictions (`store_predictions = TRUE`). Make the table from Lab 13: the out-of-fold $R^2$ for $Y$ and for $D$, the estimate, and its standard error.

    (c) By hand. Take the forest fit and its first set of folds: the cross-fitted predictions are `m$predictions$ml_l[, 1, 1]` (for $Y$) and `m$predictions$ml_m[, 1, 1]` (for $D$). Form the two residuals, compute the residual-on-residual slope $\sum_i \tilde D_i \tilde Y_i / \sum_i \tilde D_i^2$, and check it against `m$all_coef[1, 1]`. Which Week 1 result is this formula?

    (d) Which estimate do you report, by the rule from lecture? The lasso's estimate is almost the same as OLS in (a), and the forest's is not. Explain both facts.

    (e) The out-of-fold $R^2$ for $Y$ is about what Part 1 found: most of the variation in low-wage work is not predicted. Is that a problem for DML? Say what DML needs from the two predictions, and where the unpredicted part of $Y$ shows up in the result.

3.  **From one number to the ATE and the ATT.** The partially linear model reports one $\tau$. Week 6's AIPW targets the ATE or the ATT; with cross-fitted ML predictions it is `DoubleMLIRM`:

    ```{r}
    set.seed(723)
    irm <- DoubleMLIRM$new(dat,
      ml_g = lrn("regr.ranger", num.trees = 500),     ## E[Y | X], each arm
      ml_m = lrn("classif.ranger", num.trees = 500,   ## the propensity
                 predict_type = "prob"),
      score = "ATE",                 ## "ATTE" gives the ATT
      n_folds = 5, n_rep = 5,
      trimming_threshold = 0.01)     ## propensities kept in [0.01, 0.99]
    irm$fit(store_predictions = TRUE)
    e_hat <- irm$predictions$ml_m[, 1, 1]   ## cross-fitted propensities
    ```

    (a) Report the ATE and the ATT with standard errors.

    (b) Describe the distribution of `e_hat`. What share of respondents has a propensity below 0.05? Compare their means of `ability`, `parinc`, and `expect` with everyone else's. For which of the two estimands, ATE or ATT, do these respondents matter, and what is the estimate for them built on?

    (c) Order the three numbers: the ATT, the partially linear $\hat\tau$ from 2(d), and the ATE. Lecture called the partially linear $\tau$ a variance-weighted average of the effects $\tau(x)$: respondents count in proportion to $e(x)(1 - e(x))$. Use this, and your answer to (b), to explain the order. What does the order suggest about who gains more from college, those likely or those unlikely to finish it?

4.  **DML in a design: Problem Set 4 again.** In Problem Set 4 you estimated the effect of comprehensive sex-education funding on teen births with Callaway and Sant'Anna's estimator, among counties with at least 5,000 teens. With covariates, each block was an AIPW estimate built from a linear regression and a logit.

    ```{r}
    library(did); library(ddml)
    u <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wenhaojiangsoc/",
                "SOCIOL723/main/Data/sexed_county.csv")
    sx <- read.csv(u)
    sx$lrate <- log(sx$birth_rate); sx$lpop <- log(sx$pop_2010)
    big <- subset(sx, pop_2010 >= 5000)
    big <- big[order(big$fips, big$year), ]             ## sort: county, year
    Ymat  <- matrix(big$lrate, ncol = 15, byrow = TRUE) ## counties x years
    first <- big[big$year == 2003, ]                    ## one row per county
    covs  <- c("lpop", "med_hhinc_2010", "pct_pov_2010",
               "pct_black_2010", "pct_hisp_2010")
    ```

    (a) Re-estimate the linear version: `att_gt()` on `big` with the five covariates in `covs`, never-funded counties as controls, `base_period = "universal"`, and the doubly robust estimator. Report the simple ATT.

    (b) Estimate the same blocks with `ddml_attgt()` as in Lab 13: a stack of `ols` and a random forest for the change in the outcome, a stack of a logit and a random forest for the propensity. Report the simple ATT, and draw the event study, both with `lincom_weights_did()` and `lincom()`.

    (c) Compare (a) and (b) in percent. Then look at the estimates before funding in the event study. In Problem Set 4 they were flat and positive four to seven years before funding, then fell toward zero in the last two years. Did the machine-learning predictions remove that pattern? What does your answer say about what DML can repair in a difference-in-differences and what it cannot?

# Part 3: Causal Forest

## Read: "welfare" and "assistance to the poor"

Since the 1980s the General Social Survey has asked respondents whether the country is spending too much, too little, or about the right amount on a list of problems. One item on the list is worded two ways, and each respondent is assigned one wording at random: spending on "welfare", or spending on "assistance to the poor". Smith (1987, *Public Opinion Quarterly*) showed that the label alone changes the answer by a wide margin: Americans support "assistance to the poor" far more than "welfare". Green and Kern (2012, *Public Opinion Quarterly*) return to the experiment to ask *for whom* the label matters, and argue that the search over respondent characteristics should be done by a tree-based method and not by a researcher trying interaction terms one at a time.

1.  **Reading the design.**

    (a) The wording is assigned at random. What does that imply about the propensity score $e(x)$? Why can a difference in means be trusted here, when it could not be in Part 2?

    (b) Suppose the forest finds that the wording matters more for conservatives than for liberals. The wording was randomized; political views were not. Say exactly what such a finding does and does not establish.

## Run: who responds to the word?

The file holds 28,159 respondents from 1986 to 2010 with complete data. `welfare` = 1 if the respondent was asked about "welfare" (0 = "assistance to the poor"); `toomuch` = 1 if the answer was "too much". Covariates: `year`, `age`, `educ` (years of schooling), `female`, `black`, `otherrace`, `partyid` (0 = strong Democrat to 6 = strong Republican), `polviews` (1 = extremely liberal to 7 = extremely conservative), `income` (the GSS family-income category, 1 to 12), `childs` (number of children), `married`, `fulltime`.

```{r}
library(grf); library(sandwich)
u <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wenhaojiangsoc/",
            "SOCIOL723/main/Data/gss_welfare.csv")
g <- read.csv(u)
zvars <- c("year", "age", "educ", "female", "black", "otherrace",
           "partyid", "polviews", "income", "childs", "married",
           "fulltime")
X <- as.matrix(g[, zvars])
Y <- g$toomuch; D <- g$welfare
```

2.  **The average effect, and one split by hand.**

    (a) Compute the difference in the share answering "too much" between the two wordings, with its standard error. Then tabulate the share assigned the "welfare" wording by year. In which years was it not one half?

    (b) Lab 13's splitting rule: $\Delta = \frac{n_L n_R}{n}(\hat\tau_L - \hat\tau_R)^2$, with each $\hat\tau$ a difference in means. Compute $\Delta$ for three candidate first splits of the whole sample: conservative (`polviews >= 5`), `black`, and a college degree (`educ >= 16`). Rank the three. The gap $\hat\tau_L - \hat\tau_R$ is clearly largest for `black`, yet its $\Delta$ is about the same as the one for `conservative`. Why?

3.  **The forest.**

    (a) Fit `causal_forest(X, Y, D, num.trees = 2000, seed = 723)`. Report the ATE from `average_treatment_effect()` and check that it is the mean of the AIPW estimates from `get_scores()`. Summarize the forest's own propensity predictions (`cf$W.hat`). Why are they not all equal to one number, and why does the ATE differ slightly from 2(a)? (Check your explanation with a regression of `toomuch` on `welfare` and year dummies.)

    (b) Report the 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 95th percentiles of the forest's estimates $\hat\tau(X_i)$. Then run `test_calibration()`. Interpret both coefficients. Is the spread in $\hat\tau(X_i)$ real?

    (c) Each tree splits on one half of its subsample and estimates the leaf effects on the other half. If the same people did both jobs, what would happen to the spread you reported in (b), and why?

4.  **For whom does the label matter?**

    (a) Report the average effect, with its standard error, in each category of `partyid`, in each category of `polviews`, for Black and non-Black respondents, and in four schooling groups (less than 12 years, 12, 13--15, 16 or more). Describe the patterns. Which one is not monotone?

    (b) Run `best_linear_projection()` of the effect on `polviews`, `partyid`, `educ`, `black`, `age`, `income`, and `year`. Interpret the coefficients on `polviews` and `black` in a sentence each. The gap between Black and non-Black respondents in (a) is larger than the coefficient on `black` here. Why?

    (c) Rank respondents by $\hat\tau(X_i)$, largest first, with `rank_average_treatment_effect()`. Plot the TOC curve and report the AUTOC with its standard error. Read off the curve at $q = 0.2$ and say in words what that number is.

5.  **Write it up.** In one paragraph, as in a results section: the average effect of the label with its 95% interval; the evidence that the effect differs across respondents; who responds most and least, with numbers; and one sentence, following 1(b), on how the differences should and should not be read.
